director.chapterArc: A technical and physical breakthrough where Callie discovers her power is triggered by stance (feet) rather than fear or arm movement.
director.restraintNote: Maintain the narrator's grounded, observational distance. The 'magic' must feel like physics: weight transfer, leverage, and muscle memory. Do not elevate the tone to wonder; treat the discovery as a solved equation.

cues.delivery: Callie's voice is flat and analytical. She presents a logistical solution without emotion.
cues.from: "Relay it," she said. "Take the crates off at the bottom and carry them up by hand, and take the wagon up empty. She can pull it up empty. She could pull it up empty with a sore leg."
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Callie proposing the relay plan.

cues.delivery: Callie's voice is precise and technical. She explains mechanical concepts with the rhythm of a worker.
cues.from: "I carry two blocks," he said. "Double sheaves, iron-strapped, and a coil of good line. I carry them because nine hundred pounds of crates don't lift themselves onto a wagon bed, and I've used them twice in nine hundred miles and cursed the weight every other day." He tipped his head at Callie. "You'll know what they are. You came off a grain elevator."
cues.through: "A purchase," she said. "Hook the one block to the wagon and the other one up the hill, and run the fall back down. She pulls downhill on the fall and the wagon comes up. Two for one. Maybe three."
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Callie explaining the purchase system.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is steady and observational. The action of fixing the wheel is mundane competence.
cues.from: It was an ordinary job, and it was the first ordinary job Callie had done in two days, and she was so glad of it that she was nearly stupid with it. Pell had the spare down from under the bed by first light. It was a good wheel, twelve spokes, the tyre sound. The wagon was already up on its concrete blocks from the afternoon before. The broken wheel had to come off its axle nut, and the spare had to go on, and the nut had to go back and be pinned. But the spare was a finger's width wider through the hub than the old one, and it wouldn't seat.
cues.through: "It's a good hook," Callie agreed, and bolted the conduit back on, and did not feel anything in the steel at all.
cues.reason: Scene transition to routine labor; narrator must remain grounded.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is rhythmic and observational. The description of the walk establishes a calm before the training.
cues.from: They went north in the morning across the last of the flats. Callie walked out front, where she belonged.
cues.through: Callie's mother walked for the first hour. She did it with one hand on the tailgate and her hat pulled down against the sun, and she didn't say anything about the leg. After the first hour she got up on the bed with Otto's help. After the second hour she was asleep.
cues.reason: Establishing the setting and Callie's role as scout.

cues.delivery: Callie's voice is internal but spoken. She reports physical sensations with clinical detachment.
cues.from: At the noon halt Callie went down into herself to look.
cues.through: "A hand. At the bottom." Callie thought about it. "Four days, you said. The first time you emptied yourself. Before you could get a knife out of it."
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Callie reporting on her 'well' status.

cues.delivery: Pell's voice is dry and factual. He treats the ash as currency/data.
cues.from: "That's your gate," said Pell. He did not say it unkindly. He said it like a distance. He was sitting on the board with the reins in his lap and the atlas shut on his knee, and he did not pretend he had not been watching.
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Pell discussing 'gate money'.

cues.delivery: Mother's voice is quiet but firm. She asserts authority through calm logic.
cues.from: "It's hers," said Callie's mother, from the bed. She had not been asleep either. Nobody on this wagon was ever asleep. "Pell, I've known her longer than you have. She hasn't spent one thing on herself since the spring. Not one thing. If she wants to spend it on this, she's earned the right to be wrong about it."
cues.through: Pell looked at the two of them for a moment. Then he nodded and opened the atlas and wrote something small, and did not show her what.
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Mother defending Callie's choice.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is precise and tactile. The description of the 'Edge' must feel physical (cold, weight), not magical.
cues.from: They did it at the side of the road in the shade of the wagon, with the others pretending to eat and not watch.
cues.through: She stood there holding the hook, cold and empty. There was a little less water in the bottom of the well than there had been.
cues.reason: Scene transition to training; narrator must convey the mechanics of power.

cues.delivery: Katori's voice is flat and instructional. She corrects Callie with the boredom of a teacher.
cues.through: "It took me three years to choose mine. Keep the ugly shape. Stop trying to be good at it." She sat back. "Again. And this time, don't want anything. Just lean."
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Katori explaining the shape constraint.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is rhythmic and repetitive. The counting sequence must feel like a physical exertion.
cues.from: Callie leaned. The ugly shape came, the whole long useless curve of it, and she let it be ugly and held it.
cues.through: She stood there with her eyes shut for a long time. She tried to lean, the way she leaned for the Edge. The Edge came instead, the long grey sweep off the end of the hook, and she came up off it, angry, and tried again. She tried to want it. She tried to think of the horse's hoof coming up at her chest. Nothing came. She was a girl standing in a road with her eyes shut.
cues.reason: Scene transition to the failure of 'wanting' vs 'doing'. Narrator conveys the futility.

cues.delivery: Ines's voice is sparse and direct. She delivers a physical test without drama.
cues.from: "It came when she was frightened," said Ines.
cues.through: From the bed of the wagon, very faintly, came the sound of Callie's mother laughing into a blanket.
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Ines conducting the 'fright' experiment.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is observational and weary. The repetition of failed attempts builds a sense of routine frustration.
cues.from: They tried the barrow next. Callie had been sure of that one.
cues.through: "Enough," said Katori. "We need to make the scarp before dark. We'll try again tonight."
cues.reason: Scene transition to the barrow experiment; narrator conveys the futility.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is descriptive and imposing. The description of the scarp must feel like a physical obstacle.
cues.from: They made the foot of the scarp an hour before dusk.
cues.through: "Well," he said at last. "That's a hill."
cues.reason: Scene transition to arrival at the hill; narrator conveys scale.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice is precise and kinetic. The action of the crate falling must be described with physical clarity.
cues.from: They made camp at the bottom, in a lay-by at the foot of the cut where the old road had been widened for something. There was a flat patch of gravel with a low bank on the west side. Otto and Pell began unloading enough to get at the bedding, and Callie went to help, because there was nothing else to do and she didn't want to look at the hill.
cues.through: "It's not the fright," she said slowly. "And it's not my arms. It's my feet."
cues.reason: Scene transition to the breakthrough moment; narrator conveys the mechanics of stance.

cues.delivery: Ines's voice is factual. She confirms the observation without excitement.
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Ines confirming Callie didn't flinch.

cues.delivery: Mother's voice is quiet and resonant. She offers a final piece of wisdom that lands with weight.
cues.from: From up on the wagon bed, where she had been lying under a blanket with her eyes shut, Callie's mother said: "Your grandfather used to say you could stand a sack of meal on your back foot all day, if you'd only stop arguing with it."
cues.through: Above them the scarp went up into the dusk, a mile of pale road in a long straight groove to the sky, with nothing on it anywhere that a person could have hooked a block to.
cues.reason: Dialogue delivery for Mother's closing line; narrator must let the silence follow.

pauses.after: Nobody said anything for a while.
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and scene transition to mother speaking.

pauses.after: She could feel it filling now. Katori had been right. It was like feeling coming back into a foot you've sat on, a kind of fizzing ache before anything useful. At the bottom of the well there was more than a finger mark of damp now. It was the width of a hand. That was all. You couldn't draw a bucket out of it.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on the physical sensation of power returning.

pauses.after: "It's my gate money," said Callie. "It's what I was going to put on the table at Meridian, so they'd see we could pay. And if I drink it, it's gone. And I want to drink some of it anyway, because the scarp's tomorrow, and if I've got nothing in me at the bottom of the hill, I'm a girl with a hook. If I've got something in me, I might be more than that. I don't know what more yet. I want to find out while there's still time to find out." She looked at the tin. "And it's mine. It's in the book."
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and shift to Mother's intervention.
Preparation for the consequence of drinking ash.
Emphasis on physical dimension of the Edge.

pauses.before: You haven't got a better one yet.
pauses.reason: Reversal/Correction to Callie's assumption of improvement.

pauses.after: Callie counted. At forty the cold had reached her wrists. At sixty it was at her elbows. At seventy she came up off it without being told. The well had gone down by half, and she was shaking a little, and she was so hungry she could have eaten the harness.
pauses.reason: Major emotional landing on the cost of power; pause for impact.
Emphasis on the failure of 'wanting' as a trigger.

pauses.after: "If I'd told you, you'd not have been frightened. That was the whole experiment." Ines looked down at her without any pleasure at all. "Do you want me to do it again? I'll do it again. I'm good at it."
pauses.reason: Completed thought after Ines's experiment conclusion.

pauses.after: "Well," he said at last. "That's a hill."
pauses.reason: Speaker reset and scene transition to the hill description.

pauses.after: "It's not the fright," she said slowly. "And it's not my arms. It's my feet."
pauses.reason: Major realization; pause for Callie's internal processing of 'feet' vs 'arms'.
The core realization; isolation for impact.
